title: Accumulation Functions and FTC Part 1
trouble: Students forget the chain rule factor when the upper limit is a function of x.

blocks.html: Fix the left end of an interval and let the right end move. The area accumulated so far is a new function of $x$. The Fundamental Theorem says its rate of change is the height of the curve at the moving edge. This ties integrals to derivatives, and the The Chain Rule extends it.

Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 1. If $f$ is continuous and $\role[area so far]{integral}{A(x)} = \displaystyle\int_a^{\role[upper limit]{input}{x}} f(t)\,dt$, then $\role[rate the area grows]{rate}{A'(x)} = \role[height at the upper limit]{output}{f(x)}$. With a function as the upper limit: $$\dfrac{d}{dx}\displaystyle\int_a^{u(x)} f(t)\,dt = f\big(u(x)\big)\cdot u'(x)$$.

blocks.name: ftc

opts.task: Press play. When the curve is above the axis, $A$ climbs; below it, $A$ falls. Where the curve crosses zero, $A$ peaks.

blocks.cap: Top: the area under $f(t) = 2 - t$ from 0 to $x$. Bottom: that area as a function, $A(x)$. The slope of $A$ is always the height of $f$.

blocks.html: Increase $x$ by a little, $h$. The extra area is a thin strip from $x$ to $x + h$, almost a rectangle of height $f(x)$ and width $h$: $A(x + h) - A(x) \approx f(x)\,h$. So $\frac{A(x + h) - A(x)}{h} \approx f(x)$, and the approximation becomes exact as $h \to 0$ because $f$ is continuous. Area grows at a rate equal to the height of the leading edge.

blocks.title: Basic
steps: FTC Part 1: replace $t$ with $x$ in the integrand.
No antiderivative is needed (and $\sqrt{1 + t^3}$ has none among familiar functions).

blocks.title: A function in the upper limit
steps: The upper limit is $u = x^2$. Chain rule: $\cos(u)\cdot u'$.
Check: the integral equals $\sin(x^2)$, whose derivative is $2x\cos(x^2)$.

blocks.html: Forgetting the chain rule factor when the upper limit is a function of $x$: writing $\cos(x^2)$ instead of $2x\cos(x^2)$ in the second example. Check: if the upper limit is not plain $x$, there must be a factor $u'(x)$ in your answer.
